segments.title: Henry Trollope: promotion without further sea command
segments.summary: The account links Trollope's lack of further sea commands to an earlier dispute with Lord St Vincent connected with the Channel Fleet, even as Trollope continued to gain flag rank.
segments.body: Henry Trollope entered the Royal Navy in April 1771 at the age of 14. As a captain he commanded HMS Kite, Rainbow, Glatton and Russell, among other vessels, and is described here as one of the critical officers at the Battle of Camperdown. The account links the end of his sea employment to an earlier dispute with Lord St Vincent connected with the Channel Fleet. St Vincent is portrayed as unwilling to forgive the quarrel, even though Trollope's service record was too strong for him to be placed on the yellow list. Trollope stayed on the naval list and resisted retirement. He rose from Rear Admiral of the Red through Vice Admiral of the White and Red, Admiral of the Blue, and finally Admiral of the White. No further sea command accompanied those promotions.

evidence.note: Trollope joined the Royal Navy in April 1771 aged 14.

The account links an earlier St Vincent dispute connected with the Channel Fleet to the lack of further commands, describes resistance to retirement and successive flag ranks, then lists captain's commands and mentions Camperdown. Several other names in the command list are unclear and are not reconstructed.

segments.title: Researching Trollope through French-language sources
segments.summary: The French article's stronger sourcing shows why research into Trollope should follow references across language boundaries.
segments.body: The French Wikipedia article on Trollope is judged better written and better sourced than its English counterpart. Its references lead to further work on a British officer who fought against France. When an English page is thin, books and references in other languages may offer better routes into the subject. The spoken book and author names are too unclear to identify with confidence.

evidence.note: The French article is judged better than the English one, with a recommendation to consult books and other-language references. The spoken author and book titles are garbled and are not reconstructed.

segments.title: Rainbow's carronades against a new French frigate
segments.summary: Rainbow's carronade-heavy armament reflected Trollope's preference for the weapon, while its French opponent carried twenty-six 18-pounder long guns and another dozen guns.
segments.body: Trollope commanded HMS Rainbow against a newly built French frigate. The French ship carried twenty-six 18-pounder long guns and another twelve guns whose calibres are not specified. A brief, unclear remark appears to identify her as the first of her class and still being tested. Trollope favoured carronades and armed Rainbow heavily with them. He continued the practice in later commands. Rainbow's unusually heavy shot would shape the French captain's judgment once the fighting began.

evidence.note: Rainbow's opponent is a new French frigate with twenty-six 18-pounder long guns and twelve additional guns. Trollope's enthusiasm for carronades extended to subsequent commands. The French ship and captain names are unclear in the TXT.

The following account identifies the 32-pounder carronade chase guns, briefly describes the French vessel as the first of her class and being tested, and gives the captain's inference from the shot fragments. The class-status remark is unclear.

segments.title: How Rainbow's chase guns prompted a French surrender
segments.summary: A 32-pounder carronade shot led the French captain to mistake Rainbow for a disguised ship of the line and surrender after one broadside.
segments.body: The action began at 7 a.m. when Rainbow opened fire with 32-pounder carronade chase guns. One shot killed the French second-in-command. After inspecting the fragments, the French captain concluded that Rainbow was a disguised ship of the line. He fired one broadside for honour and struck his colours. Rainbow itself was a regular frigate, but Trollope had used his authority as captain to give her a heavy carronade armament. The weight of the shot made his opponent overestimate both the ship's identity and her fighting power.

evidence.note: The action starts at 7 a.m. Rainbow's 32-pounder carronade chase fire kills the opposing second captain, and inspection of the shot leads the French captain to infer a disguised ship of the line, fire one broadside and surrender.

segments.title: Trollope's final years: honours, illness and isolation
segments.summary: Trollope's victories, senior rank and honours did not protect him from illness, fear and isolation in his final years.
segments.body: After his wife's death, Trollope lived alone in Bath and had no children. Gout troubled him, and fear of burglary led him to turn his bedroom into an armoury. He was a Knight Commander and later a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath, and eventually reached Admiral of the White. For all those honours, his old age was marked by illness, fear and isolation. He died by suicide in November 1839. The account suggests loneliness and gout may have contributed, but his motives remain uncertain. The closing reflection contrasts the confidence of a younger captain, surrounded by his crew and guns, with the isolation of old age.

evidence.note: The opening gives November 2nd 1839, describes the loss of his wife, childlessness and gout, and explicitly speculates about his motive.

The later account describes isolation in Bath, fear of burglary, the bedroom armoury, gout and honours, contrasting old age with command at sea. It gives November 30 1839, conflicting with the opening day, so the public date retains only November 1839. The conjectural suicide-method detail is omitted.

segments.title: War studies and the use of history to analyse the present
segments.summary: War studies is described as applying historical knowledge and analytical skills to present problems and possible futures.
segments.body: History is described as the basis of war studies. Historical analysis does not stop when events reach the modern era; it continues up to the present. The same analytical skills can be used to examine current events and think about possible futures. Present-day analysis therefore remains grounded in historical understanding.

evidence.note: The methodological aside identifies history as the basis of war studies and describes continuing historical analysis into present events and possible futures.
